name: Kimaragang

catalog_locator: Kroeger 2008 pre-publication draft, section 2 'Vowel Harmony and Vowel Neutralization', draft p. 4 (footnote 4); published version pp. 75-88, page not verif…
catalog_quote: The pattern of stress placement in Kimaragang is slightly more complex. As in Penampang Kadazan (Miller, 1993), stress in Kimaragang seems to be neither contrastive nor fully predictable. Stress is may fall on either the penultimate or the final syllable, and in some words appears to be equally distributed over the final two syllables. Nevertheless, it is safe to say that stress always falls within the final disyllabic foot of the word, and that any /a/ occurring before the final foot is a target for neutralization.4 [fn. 4: Recall that Kimaragang /o/ is pronounced as schwa in pre-stress positions, so VN can be seen as neutralization of an unstressed vowel to schwa.]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (text layer of, header: 'Pre-publication draft of: Kroeger, Paul. 2008. Vowel Harmony in Kimaragang as a Lexical Rule.. CSLI, pp. 75-88'). The quoted passage is present verbatim on draft p.4 (lines 136-142), including the source's own typo 'Stress is may fall on either the penultimate or the final syllable', and footnote 4 ('Recall that Kimaragang /o/ is pronounced as schwa in pre-stress positions, so VN can be seen as neutralization of an unstressed vowel to schwa') is verbatim at lines 163-164. One small locator correction: the passage sits in Section 2 'Vowel Harmony and Vowel Neutralization' (draft pp. 2-5), not Section 1 (Introduction); page 'draft p.4' is right. Parallel passag…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive but not fully predictable: it falls somewhere in the final two-syllable window (penult or final syllable; sometimes roughly level over both, at least in citation forms). Kroeger 1994/2013 adds that researchers disagree on placement in particular forms, native speakers have no intuition about which syllable is stressed, and the intonational peak can land on different syllables of the same word in different contexts; e.g. rapaʔon 'to boil' is clearly final-stressed, [ˈraʔat] 'sea' penult-stressed, [araˈʔat] 'bad' final-stressed (1993:33). Non-high vowels /a, o/ reduce toward schwa before the final foot.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Kroeger 1993:33 ties the obligatory vs optional intervocalic glottal stop to final vs penultimate stress; Johansson 2011 sec. 11 describes a meaning-bearing 'stress-pitch' (high pitch with lengthening, written with circumflex) on certain words, e.g. mantad 'from' vs mâantad 'beforehand', banar 'true' vs bâanar 'in vain'. Kroeger 1993:31 flatly states 'Stress is noncontrastive' and (p.33-34) 'It is very unlikely that stress is contrastive on the word level in Kimaragang (cf. sec. 4). Assuming stress to be predictable on other grounds, stress placement will determine the environments where the glottal is phonetically optional.'
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern the word; Kroeger 1994/2013 explicitly notes judgments are for forms 'in isolation' and that intonational peaks shift by context, hinting that prominence may be partly phrasal/intonational. Variety described: Tandek (lowland) dialect, Kg. Tingkalanon (Kroeger 1993:31).
new_statements.identity_note: All Kroeger descriptions are of the Tandek (lowland plains) dialect of Kimaragang, Kota Marudu district, specifically Kg. Tingkalanon (Kroeger 1993:31); the Pitas dialect and Sonsogon (treated by Kroeger as a closely related but phonologically divergent variety; Glottolog sons1241 is listed separately) are excluded. Glottolog/Ethnologue now group Kimaragang with Tobilung and Rungus under 'Momogun' in some sources, but kima1244 = Kimaragang proper matches the variety described.

new_statements.quote: Stress is not contrastive on the word level, but it is difficult to determine what rules govern the distribution of phonetic stress. Native speakers seem to have no intuitions about stress, being unaware of stress placement in their own pronunciation and often accepting variable stress patterns for the same word as being equally correct. Marked intonational (or focal) stress can be placed on different syllables within the same word, e.g. when a story teller repeats a particular phrase or clause for emphasis. [...] Final open syllables are generally unstressed, while words ending with the suffixes -an or -on tend to have final stress. There are a few forms in which a marked focal stress seems to have become lexicalized, leading to some apparent 'minimal pairs'.

new_statements.relation_note: The listed open_url is a WRONG ITEM: the the Harvard library catalogue (DOAJ API) to Kroeger 2017 'Frustration, culmination, and inertia in Kimaragang grammar', Glossa 2(1) — already held by the project, which contains no stress/accent statement. The 2005 chapter itself is in-copyright Routledge; the archive.org scan (austronesianlang0000unse) is lending-restricted ( not reachable by automated download), so it was read via overlapping Google Books feed snippets, which chain into a continuous passage. Content: agrees with the catalog's existing Kroeger 2008 statement (stress neither contrastive nor fully predictable, penult or final) and refines it with the open-final-unstressed / -an,-on-fi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and the author cannot state a rule for where phonetic stress falls; speakers have no intuitions and accept variable placements. Tendencies only: a final open syllable is generally unstressed (so vowel-final words tend toward penultimate stress), while words ending in the suffixes -an or -on (closed final syllable) tend to take final stress. Focal/intonational stress can land on different syllables of the same word, and in a few forms a lexicalized focal stress (signalled by a pitch rise) yields apparent minimal pairs.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixed -an/-on words tend to final stress; a few forms with lexicalized marked (focal) stress giving apparent minimal pairs (the marked stress is signalled by a definite rise in pitch, unlike normal stress); one stretch of the passage ('Moreover, it is not uncommon for trained [..] stress.') was not recovered by any snippet.
new_statements.identity_note: Kroeger 2005 describes Kimaragang (Dusunic, Sabah) as spoken in the Kota Marudu / Pitas area, the same variety as the catalog's Kroeger 2008 statement; no sub-dialect is singled out in the stress passage. The the Harvard library catalogue open_url resolved to Kroeger 2017 (Glossa), also Kimaragang but not the listed work.
